description.value: The study examined whether normally distributed endogenous testosterone levels in healthy young males are associated with behavioral performance and amygdala reactivity during explicit recognition of emotional facial expressions.

design.value: A group of 21 healthy right-handed young males underwent event-related functional MRI at 3 Tesla while explicitly recognizing emotional facial expressions. Emotion and gender of poser were manipulated within subjects, and blood testosterone levels were correlated with behavioral performance and amygdala activation.

description.value: The German version was used to exclude the presence of psychiatric disorders according to DSM IV.
The battery included tasks engaging nonverbal intelligence, cognitive flexibility, visual learning and memory.
Used to measure alexithymia; no subject was alexithymic.
Blood samples were taken on the day of fMRI measurements. Assays were analyzed using an electrochemiluminescence-immunoassay (ECLIA); the sensitivity of each assay was 0.2 ng/ml.

source_definition.value: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral expressions

levels.value: anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral expressions

source_definition.value: blood testosterone levels measured on the day of fMRI measurements

description.value: Twenty-one right-handed healthy males aged 21-33 years were enrolled in the study. Participants were all students and had no psychiatric disorders, no hormone treatment, and negative drug screening.

exclusion_criteria.value: psychiatric disorders according to DSM IV
the usual exclusion criteria for MRI

recruitment_method.value: recruited by advertisements at the University of Vienna and the Medical University of Vienna, Austria

clinical_characteristics.value: Healthy young males; testosterone levels were within the normal range for 17-50 year old healthy males (2.8-8.0 ng/ml), except for one subject at 1.96 ng/ml and another at 8.17 ng/ml.

medication_status.value: Only males without any hormone treatment were included; all participants had a negative drug screening.

education_summary.value: Participants were all students (mean education 17.9 years, S.D. = 3.2).

task_description.value: Subjects viewed 72 color photographs of facial expressions portraying anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral expressions. They chose the correct emotion from two verbal possibilities presented on the left and right of the image by pressing the corresponding button on a response box using the right hand. Emotional facial expressions were presented for a maximum of 5 s with a variable interstimulus interval ranging from 12 to 18 s, during which subjects viewed a scrambled face with a central crosshair.

presentation_software.value: Presentation software package (Neurobehavioral Systems Inc., Albany, CA, USA)

instructions.value: Subjects were instructed to choose the correct emotion from two verbal possibilities presented on the left and right of the image, by pressing the corresponding button of a response box using the right hand.

stimuli.value: 72 color photographs of facial expressions portraying an equal number of the five basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness and sadness) as well as neutral expressions; both female and male faces were presented.

instrument.value: 3 Tesla Medspec whole-body scanner (Bruker Biospin, Ettlingen, Germany) at the MR Centre of Excellence, Medical University of Vienna, Austria

description.value: Gradient-recalled echo-planar imaging with 10 oblique axial slices centered on the amygdala employing asymmetric k-space sampling; FOV = 25 cm × 21 cm, matrix size 128 × 91, slice thickness 2 mm, slice gap 0.5 mm, TR = 1000 ms, TE = 31 ms.

Functional data were preprocessed using SPM2. Images were slice timing corrected, realigned to the mean image, normalized into standardized stereotactic space, and spatially smoothed using an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a full-width-at-half-maximum of 9 mm.

steps.value: spatial smoothing using an isotropic Gaussian kernel with a full-width-at-half-maximum of 9 mm

hrf_model.value: canonical hemodynamic response function and its temporal derivative

model_settings.value: Each stimulus was modelled with a separate regressor based on the individual response period. Regressors of each valence were pooled to assess brain responses to each emotion, leaving a minimum of 12 stimuli per category.
Contrast images from all subjects were included in a second level random effects analysis.
Emotion and gender of poser were within-subjects factors. Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-values were used for all ANOVAs and post hoc results were Bonferroni corrected.

estimator.value: Greenhouse-Geisser correction; Bonferroni correction for post hoc results

model_settings.value: Emotion and gender of poser were within-subject factors. Whole slab analysis and direct comparisons were presented at p < .001 uncorrected.
Emotion, gender of poser and laterality were applied as repeated factors to mean parameter estimates extracted for left and right amygdala ROIs. Greenhouse-Geisser corrected p-values are presented.
Correlation analyses between behavioral parameters and hormone level were performed across the whole sample and corrected for multiple correlations.

Correlation analysis was performed for each emotion between testosterone level and mean parameter estimates within the amygdala, provided by ROI analyses, across all participants. Results were corrected for multiple correlations.

definition.value: Male expressions of fear were significantly better recognized compared with the corresponding female expressions, whereas female expressions of disgust were recognized more accurately than the male ones.

interpretations.value: Fearful male expressions and female expressions of disgust were better recognized than their corresponding counterparts.

definition.value: Positive association of testosterone with activation during processing of angry male expressions relative to the implicit baseline.

baseline.value: scrambled face with a central crosshair

interpretations.value: Correlation analyses revealed significant associations of testosterone with activation of the inferior frontal gyrus during processing of angry male expressions.
